source.title: A is for Absorption: Studying Feature Splitting and Absorption in Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: David Chanin; James Wilken-Smith; Tomás Dulka; Hardik Bhatnagar; Satvik Golechha; J. Bloom

record.tranche_reason: The study directly measures feature splitting and presents evidence that hierarchical features can instead be absorbed, leaving apparent parent features with missing activations.
record.gate_note: The paper reports a direct feature-splitting example and several absorption experiments. General precision/recall and first-letter editing results are not included unless they directly measure splitting or absorption. The detailed values in Figures 8 and 9 are not stated numerically in the text.
record.test_reason: The study's toy and Gemma/Llama/Qwen SAE results show hierarchical features absorbed instead of cleanly split, so it bears directly on V4 and on the sparsity-objective cause in V6. It is an original source for this claim set, so no verdict labels are given.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors show hierarchical co-occurrence makes sparsity optimization favour absorption, where specific latents take over a general feature's direction and the parent latent misses cases. They find this in every LLM SAE they tested (Gemma Scope, Llama, Qwen; L1, JumpReLU, TopK). They state their results 'suggest' that varying SAE size or sparsity is insufficient to fix it, which is softer than the record's 'argue'.
record.recipe_differences: The paper measures split-feature classification and absorption using k-sparse probes, cosine alignment, and causal ablations, plus toy SAE training. It does not reproduce a matched smaller-versus-larger dictionary comparison.
record.method_sensitivity: Absorption rates vary with SAE width and L0: the text reports higher rates in wider and more sparse Gemma Scope SAEs. The empirical metric is limited to Gemma 2 2B layers 0–17.

fits_no_version.finding: SAE first-letter latents show a precision/recall trade-off with L0, and no SAE latent matches LR probe F1.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Single SAE latents are worse classifiers than linear probes for simple features, with precision and recall depending on sparsity.

record.problems: The authors describe the absorption metric as conservative and likely an underestimate: it requires a single dominant absorbing latent and fully inactive main latents, so it misses multiple absorbing latents and partial absorption. The metric's causal-ablation requirement prevents its use past layer 17 for Gemma 2 2B. The paper also notes that compute constraints limited the number of non-JumpReLU SAEs trained and evaluated.
record.rows_left_out: No directly relevant reported result was left out.

untested.parts: Matched features are not tracked across smaller and larger dictionaries, so coverage of the same inputs and nearness of direction are untested.
Not tested: the cross-model results concern absorption, not size-driven splitting.
Not tested: no nested families or concept hierarchy geometry are measured.
Not tested: no decomposition of larger-SAE latents into smaller-SAE latents, and no count of novel latents.
Matryoshka or other hierarchy-aware objectives are not tested. The sparsity-objective cause is shown only in toy models and a proof.

missing.what: Analytical proof that delta-absorption keeps reconstruction perfect while sparsity loss falls as -p11 times delta.
Robustness of the absorption rate to a mean-logit versus max-logit metric: the curves are nearly identical, and the mean version is slightly more conservative.
Absorption rate varies widely by letter across SAEs.

record.verdict_notes: This study is an original source (arXiv:2409.14507), so no verdict labels are assigned. Its absorption metric is described as conservative: it misses partial absorption and multiple absorbing latents, and it is limited to Gemma layers 0-17. The split measure (a k-sparse probe F1 jump above 0.03) is plotted against L0, not width, so it does not address V1 as stated.

versions.untested_parts: It does not track a matched feature across smaller and larger dictionaries to establish that the larger dictionary replaces it with features covering the same inputs and lying near its direction.
The cross-model and open-SAE results concern absorption, not whether the size-driven splitting pattern holds at scale.
No nested families of split features or hierarchy of concepts in model representations are measured.
The empirical absorption metric is limited to Gemma 2 2B layers 0–17; the paper does not establish that every hierarchy in every model has this behavior.
The study does not test whether larger-SAE latents decompose into combinations of smaller-SAE latents or whether larger SAEs add novel latents.
The study tests L1 and TopK-style sparsity and hierarchical toy inputs, but not Matryoshka SAEs.

rows.subject: 4-feature toy model
rows.operation_detail: Train an SAE on independently firing orthogonal features.
rows.measure: Recovery of true features; encoder and decoder alignment
rows.value: The SAE recovered one latent per true feature, with decoder representations matching the true directions and encoder features separating them.
rows.note: Null comparison for the hierarchical toy setting.
rows.check: This is a control with no absorption under independent features. It bears on V4 and V6 as the contrast showing that hierarchy, not the objective alone, triggers absorption.

rows.subject: 4-feature toy model
rows.operation_detail: Train an SAE on orthogonal features with one child feature that only fires with its parent.

conditions.value: feature 1 fires only when feature 0 fires

rows.measure: Encoder and decoder alignment with true features
rows.value: The parent latent had a recall hole when the child was active; the child latent absorbed the parent direction. The other two independent features were recovered normally.
rows.note: The paper says the hierarchical solution preserves reconstruction while increasing sparsity.

rows.subject: 4-feature toy model
rows.operation_detail: Train with variable parent-feature firing magnitude.
rows.measure: Parent-latent activation under parent-and-child feature firings
rows.value: The parent latent fired weakly when both features had magnitude 1.0; when parent magnitude was 0.75, it turned off.
rows.note: The authors call this partial absorption.

rows.subject: 4-feature toy model

conditions.value: child co-occurs with parent 95% of the time and fires alone 5% of the time

rows.note: The authors describe this as partial absorption despite imperfect co-occurrence.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B
rows.operation_detail: Measure latent activations on first-letter prompts for tokens beginning with S.
rows.measure: Firing of the apparent “starts with S” latent and a token-aligned latent
rows.baseline: Other tested tokens beginning with S
rows.value: The main latent 6510 did not activate on _short; token-aligned latent 1085 activated instead.
rows.note: The paper identifies this as a case of absorption.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B
rows.operation_detail: Measure decoder cosine similarity with the first-letter probe.
rows.measure: Cosine similarity of decoder directions with the “starts with S” probe
rows.note: The paper says latent 1085 activates at about five times the magnitude of latent 6510 on _short, contributing a similar amount of the probe direction.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B
rows.operation_detail: Ablate each SAE latent and measure the effect on the first-letter logit metric.
rows.value: Latent 1085 had a dramatically larger ablation effect than the other latents; the text gives no numeric value for this experiment.
rows.note: The authors infer that latent 1085 causally carries the first-letter information for _short.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B
rows.operation_detail: Project the first-letter probe direction out of latent 1085 before ablation.
rows.baseline: Ablation effect before removing the probe direction
rows.value: After the probe component was removed, latent 1085 no longer had a significant ablation effect.
rows.note: Supports the authors' interpretation that the latent's probe-aligned component carries the behavior.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B
rows.operation_detail: Use k-sparse probes over SAE latents to classify tokens starting with L.
rows.value: The k=2 probe showed a significant F1 increase; the text says the jump was around 0.08.
rows.note: The two latents align with lowercase l and uppercase L, respectively.
rows.check: This is a lowercase/uppercase L split within one 16k SAE. It does not compare dictionary sizes, so it cannot show V1's size-driven replacement of a coarse feature.

relation.reason: Its own toy and LLM SAE results bear directly on V4 and V6.

tranche.reason: As the V4 original, it argues that hierarchical splitting is not clean (absorption) and backs this with toy and LLM results. T2 would also be defensible.

source_check.notes: The record matches the text. The absorption metric is a conservative under-estimate and is limited to Gemma layers 0-17. The mean-vs-max-logit check (A.10, Fig 21) covers only Gemma Scope layers 0-3. Section 5.3 also reports feature splitting in Gemma Scope (Table 1, Fig 8), which no V1-V3 verdict reflects.
